beads.title: tnet login takes three flags where Go's login takes the whole up flag set
beads.description: Go's `login` is not a thin re-auth verb: `loginCmd.FlagSet` is `newUpFlagSet(effectiveGOOS(), &loginArgs, "login")`, i.e. the *entire* `up` flag set — `--hostname`, `--advertise-routes`, `--advertise-exit-node`, `--advertise-tags`, `--advertise-connector`, `--accept-routes`, `--accept-dns`, `--exit-node`, `--exit-node-allow-lan-access`, `--shields-up`, `--ssh`, `--operator`, `--report-posture`, `--timeout`, the four workload-identity flags, and the per-GOOS Linux/Windows router flags — plus `--nickname`, which `newUpFlagSet` registers only when `cmd == "login"`. It withholds exactly four: `--json`, `--reset`, `--force-reauth` and `--accept-risk`, which are `up`-only because "all login commands trigger a reauth". `loginCmd.Exec` then calls `localClient.SwitchToEmptyProfile(ctx)` before `runUp(ctx, "login", args, loginArgs)`, so a Go `login` starts a NEW profile and applies the prefs the command line named. This fork's `Command::Login` carries `--authkey`, `--authkey-file` and `--login-server` and nothing else; `run_login` (src/bin/tnet.rs) builds a `Request::Up` with every pref override hard-coded to `None`, and there is no switch-to-empty-profile step, so `tnet login` re-authenticates the *current* profile. Two consequences: `tailscale login --hostname=build-01 --advertise-exit-node --nickname work` copied from a runbook exits 2 at argument parsing, and even the flags that would parse cannot reach a fresh profile. A third, smaller one is already visible: `run_login` refuses outright when `is_ssh_over_tailscale()`, but Go's `login` registers no `--accept-risk` (that flag is `up`-only), so this fork's refusal has no override and `tnet login` over a Tailscale SSH session is simply impossible. Decide whether `login` shares `up`'s flag struct minus Go's four exclusions (and whether `--nickname` stops being hidden on `login` the way Go registers it), and whether the LocalAPI grows Go's `SwitchToEmptyProfile` given this fork's profile model, where a profile is created by switching to an unused id (tsd-91w). Port the refusals with it: `login` inherits `up`'s `--exit-node-allow-lan-access can only be used with --exit-node` check via `runUp`.

beads.title: Nothing in tnet answers Go's isRunningOrStarting gate, so status and ping run on a stopped node
beads.description: `isRunningOrStarting` (cmd/tailscale/cli/status.go) maps the backend state to a human line and an ok flag: `Stopped` -> "Tailscale is stopped.", `NeedsLogin` -> "Logged out." plus a "\nLog in at: <url>" line when `st.AuthURL` is set, `NeedsMachineAuth` -> "Machine is not yet approved by tailnet admin.", anything unrecognised -> "unexpected state: <s>", and `Running`/`Starting` -> ok. Six commands gate on it and `os.Exit(1)` when it says no: `status` (status.go, human path only — `--json` and `--web` return before the gate), `ping` (ping.go), `nc` (nc.go), `switch` (switch.go, for the states its own switch doesn't name), `serve` (serve_legacy.go) and two `debug` verbs (debug.go). `status` additionally prints its `# Health check:` block before the description when the state is `Starting` or `NoState` and `st.Health` is non-empty, precisely because that is when the health lines explain the state. None of those four strings exists anywhere in this fork: `tnet status` on a stopped node prints an empty peer table and exits 0, `tnet ping` on a logged-out node goes on to issue the ping, and `tnet nc` dials the LocalAPI socket without ever asking for status. The `# Health check:` renderer is already ported (src/bin/tnet.rs) — it is only ever reached on the running path, so the branch Go wrote it for is unreachable here. The daemon already returns the state string on every `Request::Status`, so this is pure CLI wiring: one shared helper, six call sites, exit 1. Decide whether the gate lands on all six commands at once or only the three that clearly need it, and whether `switch`'s partial version (which handles `NeedsLogin` and `Running` itself before falling through) is folded in or left alone. `nc`'s two argument refusals belong to the same call site and are also missing: Go returns `usage: tailscale nc <hostname-or-IP> <port>` when it does not get exactly two arguments and `invalid port number %q` for an unparseable port, where this fork's `port: u16` hands the user clap's wording.

beads.title: up and set never run Go's advertise-routes warnings, so a subnet router boots silently misconfigured
beads.description: `warnOnAdvertiseRoutes` (cmd/tailscale/cli/up.go) runs after every `up` and `set` whose prefs carry a non-empty `AdvertiseRoutes` or `AppConnector.Advertise`, and emits up to two warnings: `localClient.CheckIPForwarding(ctx)`, and — on Linux only — `localClient.CheckUDPGROForwarding(ctx)`. The first is the sysctl readiness probe; the second is `net/netkernelconf.CheckUDPGROForwarding`, which reads ethtool features on the TUN and the default-route interface and warns when `tx-udp-segmentation` is on for the TUN but the default interface lacks `rx-udp-gro-forwarding` or still has `rx-gro-list`, because that combination silently costs a subnet router or exit node most of its UDP forwarding throughput. This fork has the first check and never calls it from `up`/`set`: `src/ipforward.rs`'s `forwarding_warning` is wired to `Request::CheckIpForwarding` in `src/server.rs` and reachable only through `tnet debug check-ip-forwarding` — and that subcommand's own rustdoc (src/bin/tnet.rs) already tells the reader it is "normally run internally by `up`/`set`", which is not true here. So `tnet up --advertise-routes 192.0.2.0/24` on a Linux box with `net.ipv4.ip_forward=0` says nothing, where `tailscale up` prints the warning and the https://tailscale.com/s/ip-forwarding pointer this fork already carries. The GRO half has no counterpart at all — no ethtool feature read, and neither of Go's two LocalAPI verbs (`check-udp-gro-forwarding`, `set-udp-gro-forwarding`). Wiring the existing warning into `up`/`set` behind Go's exact condition is small and should not wait on the rest. The decision is the GRO half: whether an ethtool ioctl path is in scope for a fork whose TUN mode is feature-gated, and — if it is — whether the LocalAPI grows only the read or also Go's `set-udp-gro-forwarding` mutator, which changes an interface the daemon does not otherwise own.

beads.title: Four of tnet's duration flags take bare integers where Go takes a duration string
beads.description: Go registers nine `DurationVar` flags across the CLI, and every one of them parses with `time.ParseDuration`, so `30s`, `1h30m` and `250ms` are all valid and a bare integer is a parse error. Four of them exist in this fork under a different grammar: `up --timeout` (up.go, "maximum amount of time to wait for tailscaled to enter a Running state; default (0s) blocks forever") is `--timeout SECONDS` here, an integer; `wait --timeout` (wait.go, "how long to wait before giving up (0 means wait indefinitely)") is likewise integer SECONDS; `netcheck --every` (netcheck.go, "if non-zero, do an incremental report with the given frequency") is integer SECONDS; and `ping --timeout` (ping.go, default `5*time.Second`) is integer *milliseconds*, so `tnet ping --timeout 5` means five milliseconds where `tailscale ping --timeout 5s` means five seconds — the one case where a copied command line does not fail loudly but quietly means something ~1000x smaller. The other five Go duration flags are on commands or verbs this fork does not ship (`debug component-logs --for`, `debug set-expire --in`, `debug portmap --duration`) or are already tracked (`file cp --update-interval`, tsd-52k). Nothing here needs inventing: `src/goduration.rs` already ports `time.ParseDuration` faithfully — sign, fractions, `us`/`µs`/`μs`, multi-unit strings and Go's own error wording — and is already used for `cert --min-validity`, which is the one duration flag this fork got right. The decision is back-compat: whether a bare integer keeps working as an alias (kind to anyone scripting against this fork today, but it makes `ping --timeout 5` ambiguous between 5ms and Go's 5s) or is refused with Go's `time: missing unit in duration "5"`, which is the faithful port and a visible break. Decide it once for all four rather than per flag.

beads.title: tnet has no completion subcommand, so no shell can tab-complete it
beads.description: `ffcomplete.Inject` (cmd/tailscale/cli/ffcomplete/complete.go), called from `newRootCmd`, adds a top-level `completion` command with `bash`, `zsh`, `fish` and `powershell` subcommands (ffcomplete/scripts.go) that print a shell script to stdout — `. <( tailscale completion bash )` is the documented usage — plus a hidden `__complete` verb the generated script calls back into, which prints one candidate per line followed by `:<directive>`. Both take `--flags` and `--descs`. It is not only static: commands register dynamic completers, so `tailscale nc <TAB>` offers live peer DNS names via `ffcomplete.Args(ncCmd, ...)` -> `completeHostOrIP`, which reads `localClient.Status`. This fork ships no `completion` command in any form and carries no completion generator in `Cargo.toml`, so `tnet <TAB>` completes nothing in any shell. This is the reason a command-level sweep keeps missing it: `completion` is injected after the `Subcommands` literal in cli.go, so it never appears in the list a reader diffs against. The static half is cheap — `clap_complete` generates all four shells straight off the existing `Cli` derive — and the decision is how far to go: static scripts only (one new dependency, no daemon round-trip, no peer-name completion), or Go's dynamic `__complete` protocol as well, which is what makes `nc`/`ping`/`ssh` complete real peer names and needs a hidden verb plus a status round-trip on every tab. Weigh the dependency against tsd-6y1: `clap_complete` is published and would land in the daemon's crates.io graph.

beads.title: There is no health tracker, so status Health can only ever carry the captive-portal line
beads.description: Go's `health` package is a registry of `Warnable`s that components mark healthy or unhealthy, and `health.Tracker.Strings()` is what fills `ipnstate.Status.Health` — the list `tailscale status` prints as `# Health check:` and `watch-ipn-bus` streams. `health/warnings.go` alone registers twenty: update-available, security-update-available, unstable-version, network-status, ipn-state, local-log, login-state, not-in-map-poll, no-derp-home, no-derp-connection, derp-timeout, derp-region-error, no-udp4-bind, map-response-timeout, tls-connection-failed, magicsock-receive-func, warming-up, apply-disk-config, ip-forwarding and a test warnable; more are registered outside it (`dns-read-os-config-failed`, `dns-set-os-config-failed`, `resolv-conf-overwritten`, `invalid-packet-filter`, `nosnat-with-advertised-exit-node`, `ssh-unavailable-selinux-enabled`, `no-tailnet-lock-state-dir`, `blockblame-mitm-detected`, `sync-disabled`). This fork has no tracker at all — `src/ipn/mod.rs` says so in as many words — and `StatusReport.health` (src/localapi.rs) is a `Vec<String>` that holds at most one entry, the captive-portal warning raised by the loop in `src/ipn/mod.rs`. The renderer is not the gap: `tnet status` already prints Go's exact `# Health check:` block. What is missing is everything that would put a line in it. Split the set honestly before building anything. Daemon-buildable today: ipn-state, login-state, warming-up, apply-disk-config, ip-forwarding (the check already exists, see the `warnOnAdvertiseRoutes` gap) and the two update warnables (`tnet update --check` already asks the same question). Engine-gated: every DERP, magicsock, map-poll and packet-filter warnable, because the engine exposes no health signal for them — that is an engine ask, and it is also what would let the captive-portal loop stop polling and re-arm off health events the way Go does. Decide whether to build a small tracker over the daemon-buildable subset and file the ask for the rest, or to declare the one-element Health list a documented reduction and stop there; leaving it undecided is what lets a fork status page look healthy while it is not.
